events.excerpt: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027). At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system. While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework ( CVE-2026-108398 ) was publicly disclosed prior t
events.headline: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, Hi everyone, my name is Dorin, and I’m a student from Bucharest, Romania. For a university course project, I’m exploring whether a blockchain could be used to record the chain of custody of criminal evidence, so that no one could quietly alter a record after the fact. While working on it, I realized that the cryptography is the easy part; the harder question is who decides the rules. That led me to Optimism, which I chose as my case study because it has one of the most openly documented governance histories in the space. I’ve spent the past few weeks going through the Operating Manual’s version history, Agora votes and forum threads, and there are a few points I’d really appreciate help understanding. (Disclosure: I used AI tools to help with parts of the research.) Working Constitution. Section 1 limits the Working Constitution to no more than four years from its adoption, which by my reading ended around April 2026. In April, the Foundation said it would postpone any major update. Is the Working Constitution still considered in force today, and if so, on what basis (for example, an amendment under Section 3)? Is there a timeline or a process for the Bedrock Constitution? How rule changes take effect. The Operating Manual says its procedures take effect when release
events.headline: Student research on Optimism governance: questions on the constitution, rule changes and token value

events.excerpt: Why we’re posting. Proposals that put DAO money into liquidity pools often quote the pool’s fee rate (APR). We want to show, with real numbers, why that rate on its own can’t tell you whether the pool made money, and to suggest three simple questions anyone can ask when they see one. This isn’t about any particular proposal, and nobody paid for it. The short version. A pool’s fee rate only counts the money coming in. It leaves out what you lose when prices move. In our data, that loss took back all of the fees on Ethereum-style chains, and about half of them on Solana. What the fee rate leaves out When you put two tokens into a pool, you earn trading fees. That part is real, and it’s what the fee rate shows. But when one token’s price falls, the pool automatically ends up holding more of that token. So compared with simply keeping your two tokens in a wallet, you lose some money. The fee rate never shows this loss. It can’t go below zero. So we measured both parts together on real pool history: fees earned, minus the loss from price moves , compared with just holding the two tokens. 1. Same period, two very different results. Both rows cover January 2025 to July 2026. Each pool counts equally. pools fees loss from price moves what was left Ethereum-style chains (Ethereum, BSC, Ba
events.headline: Before you trust a pools fee rate (APR): what real pool history shows

events.excerpt: What's Changed Highlights Faster compilation and diagnostics. A series of optimizations across parsing, semantic analysis and lowering: module discovery (including plugin expansion) is now warmed up in parallel, the red-tree arena is built in place and chunked per item, trait-solving lookup contexts and code-size estimation are memoized, calls that would be inlined are no longer specialized first, and hash containers use foldhash. Diagnostics on large Starknet projects improved by up to ~40%. See Optimizations below. Build-independent Sierra output. The function chosen to carry the withdraw_gas check in a recursive cycle, and the order of impl candidates and impl type bounds, are now determined by a structural order instead of salsa internal ids, so the same program always compiles to the same Sierra regardless of parallel warmup. #10437 #10436 Rustc-style names for generated functions. Closures and loops are named {closure#N} / {loop#N} under their defining function (e.g. test::foo::{closure#0}::{loop#0} ) instead of by source location, keeping Sierra debug names stable across edits. The Sierra parser accepts the new form alongside the old ones. #10359 #10360 Shorter diagnostic paths. Types, traits, impls and generic arguments in type mismatch, trait resolution and inference dia

events.excerpt: A 21-property attempt combining Certora Prover, Halmos, Foundry, mutation discrimination, historical regression testing, and deployed-bytecode binding. A special thanks to Certora, Halmos, and Foundry for making these tools available. And thank you to pegaslint and the agentic Closed_Models that made it possible. We performed an independent property_driven assurance campaign against Diamond PAU, including formal verification where tractable , symbolic and concrete production-path analysis, deployed_runtime binding, targeted mutation discrimination, and replay of five (5) historical regression classes. No live Diamond PAU vulnerability was established within the tested scope. Several properties remain explicitly unresolved because the formal models were not trustworthy or tractable enough to support stronger claims. This work is not : a claim that Diamond PAU is vulnerability-free; a universal formal verification of the system; a substitute for future review after code or configuration changes. Public assurance repository: pegaslint/diamond-pau-formal-assurance Why we did this Following the many high_profile exploits across crypto, we were inspired by the words of NEAR co-founder Ilia Polosukhin who believes formal verification can be an important part of reducing vulnerability ri
events.headline: Diamond PAU: Independent Formal Assurance and Adversarial Verification using Certora Prover, Halmos, & Foundry

events.excerpt: Version 3.4.1 of xrpld , the reference server implementation of the XRP Ledger protocol, is now available. This emergency release for security-sensitive issues in the XRPL protocol was previously published as binary-only packages on 2026-09-26. This release introduces a new amendment, fixBatchV1_2 , with the default vote set to "Yes". The amendment also contains other fixes for security and stability. events.excerpt: The Ethereum Foundation has established a dedicated post-quantum research team, and the Strawmap/Lean roadmap targets hash-based signatures across the protocol stack. As the largest single manager of validator signing keys on Ethereum (~9M ETH), Lido’s exposure to quantum-vulnerable BLS keys is proportionally the largest in the ecosystem. This pre-proposal suggests forming a small working group to (1) inventory Lido’s key-management exposure, (2) draft a migration playbook aligned with protocol-layer PQ work, and (3) coordinate with the EF PQ team so that Lido node operators are migration-ready well before any hard fork mandates it. Motivation Ethereum’s consensus layer relies on BLS signatures over BLS12-381, which are not resistant to quantum attacks. While protocol-level migration is an EF/domain concern, the operational burden of key rotation at scale falls on staking infrastructure providers — and no entity carries more of that burden than Lido. events.excerpt: Content This release reduces memory use and makes tx event searches cancellable. It addresses out-of-memory crashes on nodes serving GET /cosmos/tx/v1beta1/txs (and CometBFT RPC tx_search) for queries that match a very large number of transactions. This is a non-consensus release . The state machine is unchanged, so nodes can upgrade at any time with a rolling restart. No upgrade height or governance proposal is needed. Bug fixes Tx search loads only the requested page. Previously the kv indexer loaded every matching transaction into memory before taking out the requested page, even for limit=100. It now sorts and pages matches using the index keys and loads only the transactions on the requested page. In benchmarks with 100k matches, peak memory fell from 459 MB to 45 MB and latency from 474 ms to 95 ms. ( crypto-org-chain/cometbft#69 ) Tx searches stop when the client disconnects. GetTxsEvent and GetTx called CometBFT with a background context, so a search kept running after the client had timed out or disconnected. The request context is now passed through, and the search stops when the request is cancelled. ( crypto-org-chain/cosmos-sdk#1878 )

events.excerpt: [CONSTITUTIONAL] AIP: Update Arbitrum One and Nova L1-Pricing Parameters for Ethereum Glamsterdam Abstract This proposal updates the parentGasFloorPerToken and perBatchGasCharge parameters on Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova in response to Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade. Glamsterdam changes the Ethereum gas costs associated with posting Arbitrum chain batches. Without corresponding parameter updates, the L1 fee paid by Arbitrum One and Nova users may no longer accurately reflect the cost of posting batches to Ethereum. The proposal authorizes targeted updates to the live parameters through the ArbOwner precompile. It does not introduce an ArbOS software upgrade or change the underlying L1-pricing algorithm. Motivation Arbitrum’s L1-pricing system estimates Ethereum gas cost of each batch, then uses that estimate to set the L1 fee paid by Arbitrum users and the amount the batch poster is paid back. Two parameters feed into this estimate: parentGasFloorPerToken , which mirrors Ethereum’s minimum gas charge for calldata; and perBatchGasCharge , which represents a fixed component of the estimated Ethereum gas cost attributed to each batch. The existing values reflect Ethereum’s pre-Glamsterdam cost structure. Following Glamsterdam’s activation, they may no longer accurately account for

events.excerpt: Since the DVP upgrade, ArbitrumDAO’s quorum is set as a share of delegated voting power: 50% for constitutional and 40% for non-constitutional proposals. This stopped token unlocks from pushing quorum up, but it moved the problem rather than solving it. Every delegated ARB that never votes now raises quorum without adding turnout, so incentives that reward delegation without checking whether that voting power is actually used can make quorum harder to reach. ABSTAIN votes count toward quorum and can carry thin proposals over the line, a large holder can delegate and stay silent to stall decisions, and lowering quorum again would make attacks cheaper. One possible answer is a neutral participation pool. The DAO funds it per epoch in advance, never per proposal, so nobody can buy turnout for their own vote. It pays only for votes actually cast: the same for FOR and AGAINST, less for ABSTAIN, with a cap per address. Rewards are computed from onchain VoteCast events and published as a Merkle root, so voters keep using Tally as usual. Delegates: is turnout still a real constraint after the DVP upgrade, and would a direction-neutral pool feel legitimate to you? In my free time I study consensus mechanisms and DAO governance. I’d build this as open source and may later apply for a grant
events.headline: Rewarding votes, not delegation: participation incentives under DVP quorum

events.excerpt: This release adds initial support for Fibre. Highlights Fibre client support: celestia-node now ships a built-in Fibre client, exposed under the new fibre JSON-RPC namespace on Light and Bridge nodes. Blobs are uploaded to Fibre Storage Providers and settled on-chain via an escrow-funded payment model — all driven locally by the node rather than routed through a bridge. The fibre namespace exposes: Submit — upload a blob and settle its MsgPayForFibre payment on-chain in one call. Upload — upload off-chain and settle the payment in the background. Download — retrieve a blob by its BlobID. Deposit / Withdraw — fund and unwind the escrow account that pays for storage. QueryEscrowAccount / PendingWithdrawals — inspect escrow balance and pending exits. Verified-header state client: DA nodes resolve validator sets and Fibre host addresses from the locally verified header chain (ABCI queries with Merkle-proof verification), so host discovery and payment validation don't rely on a trusted gRPC endpoint. [https://github.com/ /pull/5220 ] Requirements & notes Requires a configured core endpoint running celestia-app v10 (with the x/fibre and x/valaddr modules). Fibre is unavailable when no core endpoint is set. Breaking changes & upgrade notes Blob CLI input: blob submit now treats unprefix

events.excerpt: USDG Launches on Arbitrum as Arbitrum Joins Global Dollar Network Global Dollar (USDG), issued by Paxos, is live on Arbitrum Arbitrum has joined Global Dollar Network as one of its 150+ partners Ten partners support USDG from day one across trading, lending, collateral and on- and off-ramps. A Foundation integration programme is open to builders and a proposal before the DAO seeks to put 100M ARB and treasury assets behind USDG’s growth As a network partner, the Arbitrum ecosystem shares in the rewards earned on USDG held across it, with supply and adoption tracked publicly at arbdata.com/usdg What happened With much of Arbitrum’s activity priced in stablecoins, the choice of dollar is a strategic decision for the ecosystem. Over the past year Entropy Advisors, Offchain, the Arbitrum Foundation and Arbitrum OpCo reviewed the stablecoin landscape to inform that decision. The outcome is USDG, issued by Paxos under supervision in Singapore and the EU, backed one for one with US dollar reserves and with more than $3 billion in circulation across the networks on which it is issued. From today, USDG is natively issued on Arbitrum One with its principal uses in place at launch. It trades on Fluid and Uniswap. It earns in Morpho vaults curated by Gauntlet and Steakhouse or through syrupU

events.excerpt: Hi all, NEST has been live since 10 August ( launch thread ) and has not bought a single LDO yet. Its budget counter stood at −$542,451 at the end of September and keeps falling on most days. I spent the last few weeks building a full model of the mechanism to understand whether this can be fixed by tuning parameters. Parameter tuning alone does not solve it. The model points instead to the budget and to how profit is defined as the main levers. Below is what I propose, followed by the reasoning. The full report, model and data are linked at the end. What I propose Step 1. Now, through votes, no contract changes 1. Cut the Foundations budget for 2027 materially and, in the same vote, set the NEST threshold equal to the approved budget. I am asking for around $30M, about 30% below the current $43.8M. In the model, buybacks start to grow meaningfully from a cut of about 20% (roughly $35M), and a 30% cut roughly doubles them compared with today. The approved Foundations budget would serve as the operating baseline, not as a claim that it captures every DAO outflow; material off-budget spending, such as the $6.06M Kelp-related costs, would need to be reflected separately. 2. events.excerpt: get_historical_price: a fully empty response now lists every requested feed in missing_feed_ids, as partial responses already did. Catalog: a row whose metadata drifts from the schema keeps its symbol and pyth_lazer_id, so the feed still resolves instead of "Feed not found"; only rows without both are dropped. events.excerpt: Thirty-five years ago, a modest post on a newsgroup announced a hobby project that would forever change the landscape of modern technology. Today, we are thrilled to reflect on the impact of the Linux kernel as we share our newest report, 35 Years of Linux: The Open Source Engine of Global Infrastructure and Innovation . From underpinning the cloud to powering outer space missions, the Linux kernel has proven to be an unstoppable engine for economic growth and technical progress. And thanks to the insights from more than a dozen active contributors to the Linux kernel and numerous open source project leaders, and of course, Linus Torvalds himself, this report tells a rich story of how far the kernel has come and where it’s going on the occasion of this milestone anniversary.
events.headline: Celebrating 35 Years of Linux: The Open Source Engine Powering Three Decades of Global Innovation and Infrastructure

events.excerpt: Release v5.19.0 New Model additions EmbeddingGemma2 EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model from Google built on the Gemma 4 architecture. It encodes text, images, audio, and video, individually or combined in one input, into a shared 768-dimensional vector space for cross-modal retrieval, semantic similarity, clustering, and classification. It uses Matryoshka Representation Learning, so embeddings can be truncated to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions. It also offers configurable visual and video token budgets, and unused vision or audio towers can be disabled at load time to save memory.
